chunks: "The most common way a resistor fails is open circuit, usually from overheating.
If you dissipate more than its rating for long enough, the film or wire overheats, the value drifts, and finally it burns open, sometimes with a brown or black mark on the body.
A pulse or surge can do the same quickly: a high-energy spike can crack the film or burn through the trim spiral, even if the average power is small.
Second is drift: the value slowly changes because of heat, humidity, or aging, so a precision divider or sense resistor moves out of tolerance.
Third are mechanical failures: a cracked body or solder joint from board flexing or thermal cycling, giving an intermittent or open connection.
Chip resistors on a flexed board are a classic one.
There's also sulfur in the air, which can corrode the silver terminations of thick-film parts and open them, and moisture and contamination on high-value resistors, which show up as leakage.
A short is rare for a resistor, but it can happen through arcing over a too-high voltage, or surface contamination and dendrites in high-impedance circuits.

To prevent it I derate power to about 50 percent, check the voltage and pulse ratings, choose the right type like anti-surge or anti-sulfur parts, mind the layout so the board doesn't flex, and use conformal coating in harsh conditions."
